idea.body: A prime number has exactly two factors, 1 and itself: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, and so on. A composite number has more than two factors, and it can always be broken into primes by a factor tree. Start 12 as 2 x 6, then split 6 into 2 x 3, both prime. Every branch keeps splitting until every leaf is prime; the leaves are always the same primes, however you start the split. 1 is neither prime nor composite, since it only has one factor. A factor tree for a game score of 60 might branch into 6 and 10 first. Splitting those further gives four prime leaves: 2, 3, 2, 5.

workedExample.prompt: Build a factor tree for 90 and write its prime factorization.
steps: Split 90 into 9 x 10, two factors that are easier to work with than 90 itself.
9 is not prime, so split it further into 3 x 3, both prime.
10 is not prime, so split it further into 2 x 5, both prime.
Every branch now ends in a prime leaf: 3, 3, 2, 5.
Multiply the leaves back together to check: 2 x 3 x 3 x 5 is 90.
The prime factorization of 90 is 2 x 3^2 x 5.

figure.alt: A factor tree for 90, branching into 9 and 10, then 9 branching into 3 and 3, and 10 branching into 2 and 5.

ways.name: Factor tree
ways.when: Use this when you want to see every branch down to the prime leaves.
steps: Split 60 into two factors: 6 and 10.
6 is not prime, so split it into 2 and 3, both prime.
10 is not prime, so split it into 2 and 5, both prime.
Every branch now ends in a prime leaf: 2, 3, 2, 5.
Multiply the leaves to check: 2 times 3 times 2 times 5 is 60.
ways.trap: Stopping the tree before every leaf is a prime number.

figure.alt: A factor tree for 60, branching into 6 and 10, then 6 branching into 2 and 3, and 10 branching into 2 and 5.

frames.caption: Every branch ends in a prime leaf.

ways.name: Repeated division by primes
ways.when: Use this when you would rather divide in a straight line than branch a tree.
steps: Divide by the smallest prime that fits: 84 divided by 2 is 42.
Divide by 2 again: 42 divided by 2 is 21.
21 does not divide by 2, so try the next prime: 21 divided by 3 is 7.
7 is already prime, so stop.
The prime factors are 2, 2, 3, 7.
ways.trap: Moving to the next prime too soon, before checking it fully divides.

ways.name: The sieve picture
ways.when: Use this when you need every prime up to a limit, not just one number's factors.
steps: List every whole number from 2 to 20.
Cross out every multiple of 2 after 2 itself.
Cross out every multiple of 3 after 3 itself that is still left.
Cross out every multiple of 5 after 5 itself that is still left.
The numbers left uncrossed are prime: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19.
ways.trap: Forgetting to cross out a multiple because it looks prime at a glance.

figure.alt: A grid of numbers 2 to 20, sieved a multiple at a time until only the primes stay highlighted: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19.

frames.caption: Cross out multiples of 3 still left.
Cross out multiples of 5 still left.

bank.prompt: 7 is a prime number.
explanation: A prime number has exactly two factors, 1 and itself.
7 divides evenly only by 1 and 7.
So 7 is prime.
bank.useAgain: when you need to check if a small number has only two factors.
hints: List the factors of 7.
A prime number's only factors are 1 and itself.
bank.socraticHint: Does any whole number other than 1 and 7 divide evenly into 7?

bank.prompt: 2 is the only even prime number.

bank.useAgain: when you want to quickly rule out even numbers bigger than 2 from being prime.
hints: Check whether every even number bigger than 2 has 2 as an extra factor.
A number with an extra factor besides 1 and itself cannot be prime.
bank.socraticHint: Every even number divides evenly by 2. Why does that stop any even number bigger than 2 from being prime?

hints: Multiply each option back out to check if it equals 48.

bank.socraticHint: A prime number always has the fewest possible factors, exactly two. Does that fix its place in the order?

variant.prompt: Order these numbers by their TOTAL number of factors, fewest to most: 36, 11, 8, 20.

bank.prompt: What is the smallest prime number greater than 100?
explanation: 100 is not prime, so start testing the numbers right after it.
101 does not divide evenly by 2, 3, 5 or 7.
101 is prime, and it is the very next number after 100.
bank.useAgain: when the next prime after a round number needs to be found by testing upward.
hints: Start testing at the number right after 100, since 100 itself is not prime.
Check that number against small primes up to its square root, about 10.
bank.socraticHint: The number right after 100 is 101. Does it divide evenly by any prime smaller than about 10?

variant.prompt: What is the smallest prime number greater than 200?

bank.prompt: What is the largest prime number less than 150?
explanation: 150 itself is not prime, so start testing the numbers right before it.
149 does not divide evenly by 2, 3, 5, 7 or 11.
149 is prime, and it is the closest one below 150.
bank.useAgain: when the prime just below a round number needs to be found by testing downward.
hints: Start testing at the number right before 150.
Check that number against small primes up to its square root, about 12.
bank.socraticHint: 149 is the number right before 150. Does it divide evenly by any small prime?

variant.prompt: What is the largest prime number less than 200?

bank.prompt: What is the total number of factors of 2^3 x 5^2?
explanation: Add 1 to each exponent: 3 becomes 4, and 2 becomes 3.
Multiply those results: 4 x 3 is 12, the real total factor count.
8 comes from forgetting to add 1 to the second exponent before multiplying.
20 comes from mistakenly adding more than 1 to the exponents before multiplying.
bank.useAgain: when the add-1-then-multiply rule for counting factors gets a step skipped or a number changed.
hints: Add exactly 1 to each exponent before multiplying, no more and no less.
Multiply the two adjusted numbers together for the total.
bank.socraticHint: Each exponent needs exactly 1 added to it before multiplying. What happens to the total if you forget that step on one of them?

variant.prompt: What is the total number of factors of 2^2 x 3^3?

bank.prompt: How many prime numbers are there from 100 to 130?
explanation: Test each number from 100 to 130 against small primes up to about 11.
Only 101, 103, 107, 109, 113, 127 survive every test.
That is 6 prime numbers in the range.
bank.useAgain: when counting primes gets slower because more numbers in the range need several small-prime tests before failing or surviving.
hints: Skip every even number in the range right away.
Test the remaining odd numbers against 3, 7 and 11.
bank.socraticHint: Numbers in the 100s need testing against more small primes than numbers in the 20s. Why does that happen as numbers grow?

variant.prompt: How many prime numbers are there from 130 to 160?

stretch.prompt: 29 and 31 are twin primes, prime numbers that differ by 2. The next twin prime pair after that is 41 and 43. What is their sum?
explanation: Check that 41 and 43 are both prime: neither divides evenly by 2, 3, 5 or the other small primes below its square root.
They differ by exactly 2, so they are twin primes.
Their sum is 41 + 43, which is 84.
stretch.useAgain: when a pair of primes exactly 2 apart, twin primes, need a further calculation done on them.
hints: Confirm both 41 and 43 are prime first.
Add the two numbers together once you have confirmed they are twin primes.
stretch.socraticHint: Twin primes are two primes exactly 2 apart. What do you do with the pair once you have found them?

variant.prompt: 17 and 19 are twin primes. What is their sum?

stretch.prompt: How many prime numbers are there from 90 to 100?
explanation: Test each number from 90 to 100 for small prime factors.
Only 97 survives every test.
There is 1 prime number in that range.
stretch.useAgain: when primes get rarer in a range and most numbers there fail quickly on small prime tests.
hints: Skip every even number in the range right away.
Test the remaining odd numbers against 3, 7 and 11.
stretch.socraticHint: This range has far fewer primes than a range near 20. Why does that make sense as numbers get bigger?

variant.prompt: How many prime numbers are there from 190 to 200?

stretch.prompt: A number less than 20 has exactly 4 factors. Which of these could it be?
explanation: 6 has factors 1, 2, 3, 6, exactly 4.
9 has factors 1, 3, 9, exactly 3.
16 has 5 factors, and 25 has 3 factors.
Only 6 has exactly 4.
stretch.useAgain: when a factor-count clue rules out numbers that look similar but come from different prime shapes.
hints: List the factors of each option completely.
Only one option lands on exactly 4 factors.
stretch.socraticHint: A number with exactly 4 factors is either a prime cubed or two different primes multiplied together. Which of these options fits that shape?

variant.prompt: A number less than 30 has exactly 4 factors. Which of these could it be?

stretch.prompt: Multiply the first 5 prime numbers together: 2 x 3 x 5 x 7 x 11. What product do you get?
explanation: Multiply step by step: 2 x 3 is 6.
stretch.useAgain: when several primes need multiplying together in one long chain, one step at a time.
hints: Multiply two numbers at a time, keeping a running total.
Double check each small multiplication before moving to the next one.
stretch.socraticHint: Multiplying five numbers in a row is really just four separate multiplications. What running total do you have after the first three primes?

variant.prompt: Multiply the first 4 prime numbers together: 2 x 3 x 5 x 7. What product do you get?

stretch.prompt: There is a largest prime number.
explanation: Multiply every prime on a list together and add 1.
The result is either prime itself, or it has a new prime factor that was not on the list.
That means another prime always exists beyond any list, so there is no largest prime number.
stretch.useAgain: when a claim about primes running out or stopping needs checking against how factor trees always find a new prime.
hints: Imagine multiplying every prime on a very long list together, then adding 1.
Think about whether that new number could possibly be divisible by any prime already on the list.
stretch.socraticHint: If you multiplied every prime on a list together and added 1, could any prime already on your list divide that new number evenly?
